reference.source: Fitzpatrick's Dermatology / Rook's Textbook of Dermatology
clinicalPearls: Morphea is a localised sclerosing disorder of the skin that, unlike systemic sclerosis, spares the internal organs and is not accompanied by Raynaud phenomenon or sclerodactyly
Early plaques are erythematous or violaceous and indurated, evolving into firm, waxy, ivory-coloured centres often surrounded by a lilac inflammatory ring that signals active disease
Subtypes include circumscribed (plaque) morphea, generalised, linear, and deep forms, each with different distribution and complication profiles
Linear morphea in children can cross joints and, when it affects the limbs or face, may impair growth, cause contractures, or produce the en coup de sabre pattern on the forehead
Facial and periorbital linear disease warrants assessment for underlying neurological and ophthalmological involvement

Treatment aims to halt inflammation during the active phase, since established sclerosis and atrophy are difficult to reverse; options range from topical and phototherapy approaches to systemic immunomodulation in extensive or deep disease
Physiotherapy and monitoring for joint contractures are important in linear and deep subtypes
Distinguish morphea from systemic sclerosis clinically and, if needed, serologically, to avoid unnecessary alarm and inappropriate investigation
reference.pathophysiology: Morphea is an immune-mediated fibrosing process in which an initial inflammatory phase, characterised by a perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate and endothelial activation, is followed by excessive deposition of collagen in the dermis and, in deeper subtypes, the subcutis and fascia. Dysregulated production of pro-fibrotic cytokines and growth factors drives fibroblasts to lay down dense, thickened collagen bundles, with loss of adnexal structures and normal fat. Vascular changes and, in some cases, autoimmune associations contribute. The result is progressive induration and, later, atrophy; when fibrosis extends across joints or affects growing tissues in children, functional and cosmetic sequelae follow.
additionalDifferentials: Systemic sclerosis (must be distinguished as it involves internal organs)
Lichen sclerosus (can coexist and overlap clinically)
Chronic graft-versus-host disease with sclerodermatous features
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy, ideally deep enough to assess dermis, subcutis, and fascia, to confirm the diagnosis and subtype
Clinical assessment for systemic sclerosis features, with autoantibody testing where indicated
Imaging (including MRI) in linear or deep disease to define extent and detect muscle, bone, or CNS involvement
Ophthalmology and neurology review for craniofacial linear disease
Serial mapping or scoring of lesions to monitor activity and progression
redFlags: Craniofacial linear morphea (en coup de sabre / Parry-Romberg) with neurological symptoms, seizures, or eye involvement
Rapidly extending or deep lesions crossing joints and threatening contractures
Growth disturbance or limb length discrepancy in affected children
Extensive generalised disease causing functional impairment
Diagnostic uncertainty where systemic sclerosis cannot be confidently excluded
reference.prognosis: Many plaque-type lesions eventually become inactive over several years, leaving pigmentary change and atrophy, whereas linear and deep subtypes, particularly in children, carry a higher risk of lasting functional and cosmetic sequelae; early treatment of the inflammatory phase improves outcomes.
pitfalls: Confusing morphea with systemic sclerosis and triggering unnecessary anxiety or investigation
Missing the active inflammatory (lilac ring) phase when treatment is most effective
Underappreciating growth and contracture risk in paediatric linear disease
Failing to screen for neurological and ocular involvement in craniofacial disease
Assuming established sclerosis will respond to anti-inflammatory therapy
management: Halt inflammation during the active phase, since established sclerosis and atrophy are hard to reverse, using topical corticosteroids, topical calcineurin inhibitors or calcipotriol for limited disease and phototherapy such as UVA1 or narrowband UVB for widespread superficial disease
Systemic immunomodulation for extensive, linear, deep or functionally threatening disease, typically methotrexate with a corticosteroid bridge, or mycophenolate as an alternative
Physiotherapy and occupational therapy to prevent and manage contractures, particularly in linear disease crossing joints in children
Ophthalmology and neurology assessment for craniofacial and en coup de sabre disease
Emollients, management of atrophy and scarring, and cosmetic or reconstructive input for established sequelae
Serial lesion mapping and scoring to monitor activity and detect relapse
Multidisciplinary dermatology, rheumatology and paediatric care
